title: Ekpang Nkukwo
author: Iquo Bassey
desc: Grated cocoyam wrapped a teaspoonful at a time in cocoyam leaves, layered rather than stirred, and shaken loose after about twenty minutes — never stirred.
longDesc: Ekpang nkukwo is a technique dish and the technique is the wrapping. Six medium cocoyams are peeled, grated or blended, loosened with about half a cup of water, and then taken up a teaspoonful at a time and wrapped in cocoyam leaves — each wrap placed gently on top of the last until all the paste is used, so the pot is layered rather than mixed. After about twenty minutes you shake the pot to loosen them, and you never stir. Periwinkle, crab, dry fish and shrimp cook alongside, and the palm oil goes in near the end.
ingredients: About 1/2 cup water, to loosen the paste
750 ml water — see the note on the two figures
steps: Peel, wash and grate or blend the cocoyam, then mix in about half a cup of water to soften it further.

Using your fingers, take about a teaspoon-size of the paste at a time and wrap it in the leaves, placing each one gently in the pot. Place each wrap on top of the other until all the paste is wrapped.
Add 2 cups of water gradually and bring to the boil.
Add the fish, shrimps, crabs and seasonings and cook on low heat.
After about 20 minutes, shake the pot to loosen the wraps — do not stir.
Add the remaining water and cook 10 minutes.
Add the crayfish and cook 5 minutes.
Add the palm oil, lift the wraps gently with a spoon so it distributes, and cook 5 minutes.
Adjust the salt and cook a final 5 minutes.
chefTips: Teaspoon-size portions. Small wraps cook through; large ones stay raw in the middle.
Layer, do not mix. Each wrap goes on top of the last and the pot is built up rather than stirred together.
Shake the pot at twenty minutes, do not stir. Same logic as ikokore and kekefiyai — the parcels need to come loose without being broken.
Lift the wraps gently with a spoon when the palm oil goes in, so it coats everything without disturbing the layers.
Utasi or ntong, and the ratio is given: four utasi leaves or eight ntong. Utasi is twice as strong.

On the water: the ingredient list says 750 ml but the method calls for 2 cups and then 'the remaining water'. Two cups is roughly 475 ml, so the remaining is roughly 275 ml. The discrepancy is in the source.
Another named source wraps a tablespoon rather than a teaspoon — a threefold difference in portion size. Both are published and neither is adjusted.
commonMistakes: Wrapping portions too large to cook through.
Stirring the pot at any point.
Adding all the water at the start.
Adding the palm oil early, where it stops the wraps cooking.
Using utasi and ntong interchangeably at the same count.
servedWith: On its own, as a one-pot
sources: Adapted from 'Ekpang Nkukwo', byline '1Qfoodplatter'. Quantities as printed: 6 medium size Cocoyam; 1/2 cup unshelled Periwinkle (optional); 6 dressed Crabs (optional); 1 medium size Dry fish; 1/2 cup Fresh Shrimps; 1 cup Stock fish pieces (optional); 3 tablespoons Crayfish; 4 leaves utasi or 8 ntong leaves; Cocoyam leaves (segmented) — no quantity; 2 tablespoons dry Pepper; 2 cooking spoons Palm oil; 2 tablets Crayfish seasoning; 750ml Water; salt to taste. Yield not specified.

THE WRAPPING, close to verbatim and the reason this version is used: 'Using your fingers, take about a teaspoon size of the paste at a time and wrap in the leaves placing gently in the pot. Place each wrap on the other until all the paste is wrapped.' Note the teaspoon-size portions and the layering rather than stirring.

The timed sequence is as printed: add 2 cups water gradually and boil; fish, shrimps, crabs and seasonings on low heat; 'after ~20 minutes shake pot to loosen (don't stir)'; remaining water, 10 minutes; crayfish, 5 minutes; oil, lift gently with a spoon, 5 minutes; adjust salt, final 5 minutes.
UNIT MISMATCH, flagged: the ingredient list says 750 ml of water but the method calls for '2 cups' and then 'the remaining water'. Reproduced as printed with the arithmetic noted in the tips.

THE GRATING ENDPOINT IS CONFIRMED ABSENT, which was specifically investigated. This page says only 'Peel, wash and grate or blend the coco-yam' then mix with 'about ½ cup of water to soften it further' — no grater type, no fineness, no endpoint. The Guardian version is no better: 'Shred the cocoyam or pulse with a blender to give that grated feel', which defines the endpoint by the word being defined. Two sources, no cue. Recorded as a real gap.
DISAGREEMENT ON PORTION SIZE, not reconciled: teaspoon-size wraps here against 'one tablespoon of grated cocoyam on a torn leaf' in the Guardian version (NGA072) — a threefold difference.

MAJOR DISAGREEMENT ON PALM OIL, not reconciled: 2 cooking spoons here against '1½-2 cups palm oil/red oil' in the Guardian version. That is roughly an order of magnitude. Also 6 medium cocoyam here against 4 pounds of cocoyam and water yam there — and the Guardian adds water yam, which this recipe does not use at all.
ON ITS ORIGIN: the Guardian places the dish with the Efik and Ibibio peoples of eastern Nigeria and also with the Bakweri of Cameroon.
reheating: Low heat with a splash of water, no stirring.
healthBenefits: Cocoyam is a low-allergen starch rich in potassium and resistant starch.
Periwinkle, crab and shrimp are all very lean, high-iron proteins.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Ekpang nkukwo is the most laborious dish in the Efik repertoire and it shows: dozens of individual teaspoon-sized parcels, each wrapped by hand in a cocoyam leaf, layered into a pot and then never touched with a spoon. It belongs to the same family of no-stir techniques as ikokore and kekefiyai, where the whole skill is building something in a pot that would be destroyed by mixing.
